objective: Managing locks that block data access in Amazon Redshift and Amazon RDS

sources.cite: AWS re:Post Knowledge Center, 'Locks are blocking my queries in Amazon Redshift. How do I resolve this?'
sources.note: Read through a summarizing fetch on 2026-11-17. Relevant text: 'AccessExclusiveLock blocks all other lock attempts' (DDL such as ALTER TABLE, DROP, TRUNCATE); 'AccessShareLock blocks only AccessExclusiveLock attempts' (SELECT, UNLOAD, UPDATE, DELETE); a waiting AccessExclusiveLock request 'blocks all subsequent lock requests on the same table'; a transaction started with BEGIN stays open until COMMIT and an idle one can keep holding locks; find the holder through SVV_TRANSACTIONS (granted = f means waiting); end it with PG_TERMINATE_BACKEND; for idle sessions that hold locks, adjust session_timeout with ALTER USER. The article does not mention rebooting; the REBOOT_CLUSTER reference (read 2026-11-18) says a reboot interrupts in-progress transactions and queries, which the application must resubmit.

brief.situation: You are the data engineer at Pellow Freight, a fictional carrier. The nightly ELT job swaps the new day into analytics.shipments with a TRUNCATE and an INSERT, normally done by 06:00. This morning it is still running, and since 06:40 every dashboard that reads shipments spins. The executive review opens those dashboards at 08:00.
handover: Analysts connect with their own users from a SQL client; some leave sessions open overnight.
The ELT runs as user etl_svc from Step Functions; a restart of the job takes about 25 minutes.
howItWorks: The terminal shows each command's output; the diagram shows the warehouse, the sessions on analytics.shipments and who waits for whom.
Each command takes a minute or two; the clock moves only when you act or wait.
When you close, you write the record and explain your reasoning.

writeup.question: For the record: why the load and the dashboards waited, what you ended and why that one, and what prevents it.

parts.label: Why
parts.criteria: Reads the lock chain from holder to waiters.
parts.modelAnswer: Session 18842 opened a transaction at 17:52 yesterday, ran a SELECT and never committed, so it held an AccessShareLock on shipments. The load's TRUNCATE needs an AccessExclusiveLock, waited behind it, and every dashboard SELECT queued behind the waiting load.

parts.label: What
parts.criteria: Ends only the idle holder, after checking and telling its owner.
parts.modelAnswer: sys_query_history showed only a BEGIN and a finished SELECT, so nothing was lost by ending it. I told the analyst and ran pg_terminate_backend(18842); a reboot would have interrupted the load as well.

parts.label: Prevention
parts.criteria: Limits idle sessions where they come from.
parts.modelAnswer: A SESSION TIMEOUT on the analysts' users ends idle sessions after an hour; the team was reminded to commit or close their clients.

rebooted.headline: The whole warehouse for one session
rebooted.body: One idle session held the lock. Ending that session releases it; a reboot ends everything, including the 85-minute load you were waiting for.

reviewBlank.headline: A queue of waiters behind one idle transaction
reviewBlank.body: A waiting AccessExclusiveLock blocks every later request on the table. Find the oldest granted lock in SVV_TRANSACTIONS and end that session.

released.headline: Good: the holder, not the waiters
released.body: You found the session that held the lock, checked it was idle, told its owner, ended only it, and set a session timeout so a forgotten BEGIN cannot block a load again.

scoring.modelReasoning: Everything waits on one table: the load's TRUNCATE needs an exclusive lock, and an idle analyst transaction from yesterday still holds a shared one, so the load waits and every dashboard query queues behind the load. Check that the holder is idle (a BEGIN and a finished SELECT), tell its owner and end just that session with pg_terminate_backend. A reboot would also end the load and roll it back; more WLM slots only add waiters. Then give the analysts' users a session timeout.
